desc: This station involves taking a focused history from an older woman with right upper quadrant pain and vomiting, interpreting her abdominal X-ray, explaining why this is not cholecystitis or cholangitis, and counselling her about the diagnosis and initial plan.
explain:
Gallstone ileus

Gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by a large gallstone (usually over 2 to 2.5 cm) that has eroded from the gallbladder into the adjacent bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula, commonly into the duodenum. The stone usually lodges at the narrowest point, the terminal ileum. It typically affects older women with long-standing gallstones, and the preceding biliary symptoms are often intermittent. This is why the pain may come and go (tumbling stone) before the obstruction becomes fixed.

Rigler triad

  • Small bowel obstruction

  • Gas in the biliary tree (pneumobilia)

  • An ectopic gallstone, usually in the right lower quadrant

All three features are present in only a minority of cases on plain film, so CT is often used and is more sensitive. The finding indicates gallstone ileus from a biliary-enteric fistula, and the patient needs surgical referral for relief of the obstruction.

Distinguishing the biliary emergencies

  • Acute cholecystitis: persistent right upper quadrant pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers and a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation under the right costal margin). It is typically not obstructive.

  • Acute ascending cholangitis: Charcot triad of fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, with a cholestatic liver profile. Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion and signals severe disease needing urgent biliary drainage. Cholangitis is not simple cholecystitis.

  • Gallstone ileus: obstructive picture (vomiting, distension, constipation) with imaging showing Rigler triad. Fever and jaundice are usually absent, as in this patient.

Management

Management begins with resuscitation: nil by mouth, IV fluids, correction of electrolytes, antiemetics, analgesia and nasogastric decompression if vomiting. Nephrotoxic and risky drugs (NSAID, ACE inhibitor, metformin) are withheld while she has acute kidney injury. Definitive treatment is surgical, usually enterolithotomy to remove the stone. Whether to deal with the fistula and gallbladder at the same operation is a surgical decision, weighed against the patient's frailty and comorbidities. In an older patient, anaesthetic fears are common and should be heard and addressed, and the discussion should support informed consent and shared decision making.
focus: Acute right upper quadrant pain with suspected cholecystitis, cholangitis or gallstone ileus
guide:
A high-performing candidate takes a structured history that separates the biliary pain from the obstructive features (vomiting, constipation, no flatus). They screen explicitly for Charcot triad and for Reynolds pentad, and identify dehydration and renal risk from perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen. They request an abdominal examination and describe Murphy's sign correctly. They recognise Rigler triad on the X-ray, state gallstone ileus and explain clearly why this is not cholangitis or cholecystitis. They start fluid resuscitation, make the patient nil by mouth and escalate to the surgeons. In the counselling task they use plain language and respond with empathy to the fear of anaesthesia.

A borderline candidate recognises small bowel obstruction in a patient with known gallstones but does not name all three features of Rigler triad, or labels the picture as cholecystitis or cholangitis without justifying it. They may screen for fever and jaundice without linking them to Charcot triad, and may miss the renal risk from her medicines. They may give a reasonable explanation to the patient but use jargon and not explore her concerns about anaesthesia.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Margaret Hollis

  • Age: 74 years old

  • Gender: Female

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No

  • Setting: Emergency department

Presenting complaint: Right upper abdominal pain, then vomiting and bloating

History of presenting complaint:

  • Onset and duration: Crampy pain under your right ribs came and went for 4 days. For the last 2 days you have been vomiting and your belly has swollen up.

    • Episodes of pain last a few hours and then ease. Pain is about 5/10 at its worst, mostly colicky, sometimes goes to the right shoulder blade.

  • Vomiting: About 6 times a day, now dark green-brown and foul-smelling. You cannot keep fluids down.

  • Bowels: Last bowel motion 3 days ago. You have passed no wind for about 24 hours. Stool colour was normal before that.

  • Fever, jaundice: You have had no fevers or rigors. Eyes and skin are not yellow. Urine has been normal to slightly dark because you are dehydrated; stools were not pale. No itch.

  • Confusion, dizziness: No confusion. You feel lightheaded when you stand.

  • Urine output: Passing much less urine over the last day.

  • Prior biliary history: Gallstones were found on an ultrasound 3 years ago after similar attacks. Your GP suggested surgery and you declined because you were frightened of an operation.

  • Other: No weight loss, no chest pain, no shortness of breath. No blood in vomit or stool. No previous abdominal surgery.

Medical history:

  • Hypertension

  • Type 2 diabetes

  • Osteoarthritis of the knees

Medications:

  • Perindopril 5 mg daily

  • Metformin 500 mg twice daily

  • Paracetamol as needed

  • Ibuprofen from the pharmacy for the last 4 days for the pain (if asked specifically about over-the-counter medicines)

Allergies: Codeine causes severe nausea (intolerance, not allergy)

Family history: Sister had her gallbladder removed

Social history:

  • Widowed, lives alone in a unit; daughter lives nearby

  • Retired primary school teacher

  • Never smoked; one sherry on weekends

  • Independent in all activities of daily living

ICE:

  • Ideas: You think a stomach bug or the gallstones have flared up again.

  • Concerns: Your husband died of complications after an operation under a general anaesthetic, and you are terrified of needing surgery and of not waking up. Raise this only if asked about your concerns or when surgery is mentioned.

  • Expectations: You want the vomiting and pain to stop and you want to avoid an operation if possible.

Examiner information (give only when the candidate asks):

  • Observations: HR 98 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg (lying), postural drop to 100/62, temperature 37.2 C, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, BGL 9.8 mmol/L.

  • General: Dry mucous membranes, no jaundice, alert and orientated.

  • Abdomen: Distended and tympanic, mild right upper quadrant tenderness without guarding or peritonism, no palpable mass, no hernias, no scars. Bowel sounds are high pitched and tinkling.

  • Murphy's sign: Negative. If the candidate describes the technique correctly, report no inspiratory arrest.

  • Bloods (if requested): WCC 11.4, CRP 38, creatinine 128 umol/L (baseline 78), potassium 3.3, bilirubin and ALP normal, lipase normal, lactate 1.9.

Abdominal X-ray report (give at task 2): Dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Branching linear gas lucency over the right upper quadrant consistent with gas in the biliary tree. A 3 cm rounded calcified density in the right lower quadrant. No free subdiaphragmatic gas.

Examiner prompt in task 2 if not yet covered: 'What is Charcot triad and does this patient have it?'

The candidate may ask further questions of you; use only the provided history above. Provide a realistic answer if the candidate asks a question outside the script.

The candidate should interact with you using non-medical terminology. Please interrupt the candidate if they use medical terminology that would not be clearly understood by the lay public.
points: Murphy's sign is elicited by palpating under the right costal margin while the patient breathes in; inspiratory arrest suggests acute cholecystitis.
Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain) points to acute ascending cholangitis; Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion.
Rigler triad (small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone) indicates gallstone ileus from a biliary-enteric fistula and needs surgical referral to relieve the obstruction.
Always check for dehydration and acute kidney injury in vomiting patients, and review ACE inhibitors, metformin and NSAIDs.

stem:
You are the emergency department resident reviewing Margaret Hollis, a 74-year-old woman who has presented with 4 days of intermittent right upper quadrant pain, followed by 2 days of vomiting and abdominal bloating. Observations have been taken and an abdominal X-ray has been done.

The examiner will give you examination findings and the X-ray report when you ask for them.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient and request the examination findings you would want, including how you would test for Murphy's sign (4 minutes).
Interpret the abdominal X-ray findings provided by the examiner, state your diagnosis and explain to the examiner why the findings argue against acute cholangitis and acute cholecystitis (2 minutes).
Explain the diagnosis and your initial management plan to the patient in lay terms, and address her concerns (2 minutes).
title: Right upper quadrant pain with vomiting in an older woman
